newsitem.title: PERU: Peru relaunches hostage crisis talks with rebels.
newsitem.headline: Peru relaunches hostage crisis talks with rebels.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori's government renewed contact with Marxist rebels holding 74 captives in Lima on Friday, breaking a logjam in the 25-day crisis and raising hopes of a peaceful solution.
Government negotiator Domingo Palermo arranged a second face-to-face meeting with Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini for the weekend.
But he insisted the government would accept nothing short of the complete release of all the remaining captives at the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence.

"My goal is to free the 74 hostages in their entirety, in good health and as quickly as possible," Palermo told foreign correspondents who witnessed his four-minute, walkie-talkie conversation with the guerrilla leader.
Palermo and Cerpa were polite and good-humoured in their contact, which broke a stalemate that has lasted since the last release of hostages on New Year's Day.
Palermo also spoke by telephone with Fujimori during his nearly three-hour meeting with correspondents from Reuters, the Italian news agency ANSA, Agence France Presse and Mexican TV channel ECO.
It was the government negotiator's first contact with the media since MRTA rebels stormed the residence during a Dec. 17 cocktail party.
The guerrillas are using their hostages to pressure Peru's government into releasing about 400 jailed comrades. But Fujimori has rejected this demand.

The MRTA originally took more than 500 hostages but has released more than 430. It still holds top government and security force officials, Japanese businessmen and diplomats, and Fujimori's younger brother, Pedro.
Fujimori hailed the talk with Cerpa as a "good sign" that raised "hopeful prospects" of a bloodless end to the crisis.
"We have established a bridge via today's radio contact," he told local radio station Radio Programas.
Palermo has not met Cerpa since their only face-to-face encounter on Dec. 28 when he won the release of 20 hostages. They have kept in contact via short, handwritten messages.

"I am the contact, not the negotiator, though you could say it is the same thing," he told the correspondents. Palermo heads a government crisis team that also includes Prime Minister Alberto Pandolfi, Energy Minister Daniel Hokama and Economy Minister Jorge Camet.

A senior government source added that a provisional "guarantor committee" was being set up to supervise a possible negotiated end. The committee would include members of the government and "two or three very strong institutions or countries," the source said.
Neither Palermo nor other government sources would give details on whether the rebels would be allowed to leave the country if they lay down arms and release the captives.
About 20 MRTA rebels entered a small jungle village Friday to demand food and spread propaganda, local radio reported.

In the first such action for several months, a rebel unit of 13 men and seven women, all between 17 and 25-years-old, woke up residents of Palcazu, the central Pasco region, around dawn, Cadena Peruana de Noticias (CPN) said.
They collected food, gave speeches about the takeover of the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima, and painted slogans on walls.
"Long live the MRTA!" and "Long live the takeover of the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima" read some of the slogans, according to CPN.
The MRTA's armed members, estimated to number anywhere between a few score and 250, are mainly based in Peru's central jungle area.

The government source said the two Peruvian government ministers still held captive "want to be the last to leave ... (Foreign Minister) Francisco Tudela said: 'I want to go out last. Tell the president not to worry.'"
He added that despite early reports the rebels numbered 20 or more, "we now know there are only about 15 of them inside." He added: "There has been no torture, just a bit of swearing."

Captive Bolivian ambassador Jorge Gumucio appeared smiling and waving at a residence window on Friday afternoon after his daughter persuaded police outside to play some Andean folk music over loudspeakers for him.

Earlier Friday, the rebels fired four shots in the air before dawn in an apparent reminder to the world of their heavily armed presence. The jungle-trained rebels possess AKM assault rifles and grenades and have booby-trapped and mined the compound.
